concepts.name: Tropical Cyclone: Definition, Formation Conditions, and Energy Source
key_dimensions: Minimum Sea Surface Temperature (SST) threshold of 26–27°C and its exceptions (e.g., Medicanes forming below threshold)
Role of latent heat of condensation as the primary energy source vs. extratropical cyclones powered by temperature gradients
Coriolis force requirement: why cyclones do not form within 5° of the equator
Warm core vs. cold core structure — UPSC trap distinguishing tropical from extratropical systems

concepts.name: Global Nomenclature of Tropical Cyclones by Ocean Basin
key_dimensions: Regional names: Hurricane (Atlantic/NE Pacific), Typhoon (NW Pacific), Cyclone (Indian Ocean/South Pacific), Willy-Willy (Australia — common misconception)
WMO-designated Regional Specialized Meteorological Centres (RSMCs) and their jurisdictions
UPSC trap: 'Cyclone' is the correct term for Bay of Bengal AND Arabian Sea systems — both under IMD's RSMC New Delhi
Why the same physical phenomenon has different names — historical and jurisdictional reasons

concepts.name: IMD's Tropical Cyclone Classification Scale (Indian Ocean)
key_dimensions: Seven-tier IMD classification: Low Pressure Area → Depression → Deep Depression → Cyclonic Storm → Severe Cyclonic Storm → Very Severe → Extremely Severe → Super Cyclonic Storm
Wind speed thresholds for each category (e.g., Cyclonic Storm: 63–88 km/h; Super Cyclone: ≥222 km/h)
UPSC trap: IMD uses a different scale from Saffir-Simpson; direct mapping between the two is not straightforward
Significance of 'Deep Depression' stage — when IMD begins issuing cyclone warnings

concepts.name: Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale (SSHWS)
key_dimensions: Five-category scale based solely on sustained wind speed (Category 1: 119–153 km/h to Category 5: ≥252 km/h)
UPSC trap: SSHWS does NOT account for storm surge, rainfall, or size — common misconception that it measures overall destructiveness
Category 3–5 classified as 'Major Hurricanes' — policy/disaster management implication
Comparison with IMD scale: why India does not use SSHWS and implications for international reporting

concepts.name: WMO Tropical Cyclone Naming System: History and Current Protocol
key_dimensions: Evolution: US military phonetic alphabet (1950s) → female names (1960s) → alternating male/female (1979) → regional lists
WMO principle: pre-assigned alphabetical rotating lists maintained by each RSMC
Retirement of names: criteria (significant death toll or economic damage) and who decides — WMO Hurricane Committee vs. RSMC
UPSC trap: names are NOT given in real-time by a single global body; each basin has its own committee and list

concepts.name: Cyclone Naming in the North Indian Ocean: The 13-Nation Protocol
key_dimensions: 2020 expansion: original 8 nations (Bangladesh, India, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Thailand) expanded to 13 (adding Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Yemen)
IMD's role as RSMC New Delhi — sole authority for naming cyclones in the North Indian Ocean (Bay of Bengal + Arabian Sea)
List of 169 names (13 names × 13 countries) released in 2020 — how the list is used sequentially
UPSC trap: India does not exclusively name all cyclones; each of the 13 countries contributed names, used in rotation

concepts.name: Bay of Bengal vs. Arabian Sea Cyclone Frequency and Intensity Asymmetry
key_dimensions: Bay of Bengal receives ~80% of North Indian Ocean cyclones — reasons: warmer SST, lower wind shear, greater moisture
Arabian Sea cyclones historically weaker but trend of intensification post-2014 (e.g., Cyclone Kyarr, Tauktae) — climate change link
Role of the Somali Jet and Southwest Monsoon in suppressing Arabian Sea cyclone formation June–September
UPSC trap: Arabian Sea cyclones threaten Mumbai and Gujarat — policy relevance for NDMA; Bay of Bengal cyclones more frequent but Arabian Sea ones can be more intense

concepts.name: Cyclone Season Patterns in the North Indian Ocean
key_dimensions: Two peak seasons: pre-monsoon (April–June) and post-monsoon (October–December) — reason: monsoon wind shear suppresses cyclogenesis June–September
October–November as the most active month for Bay of Bengal cyclones historically
UPSC trap: cyclones CAN form during monsoon season (June–September) but are rare — e.g., Cyclone Nisarga (June 2020, Arabian Sea)
Climate change signal: increasing off-season cyclone formation and rapid intensification events

concepts.name: Structure of a Tropical Cyclone: Eye, Eyewall, and Rainbands
key_dimensions: Eye: calm, warm, subsiding air — lowest pressure zone; NOT the most dangerous area
Eyewall: highest wind speeds, most intense rainfall and convection — the most destructive zone
Outer rainbands: spiral precipitation bands extending hundreds of kilometres — cause flooding far from landfall point
UPSC trap: eye diameter vs. storm diameter — a small eye does not mean a small or weak storm; can indicate an intense, compact system

concepts.name: Rapid Intensification (RI) of Cyclones: Definition and Drivers
key_dimensions: WMO/NHC definition: increase in maximum sustained winds of ≥55 km/h (30 knots) within 24 hours
Key drivers: warm ocean heat content (OHC) at depth, low vertical wind shear, high mid-level moisture, favorable outflow
Climate change link: warming oceans enabling RI events closer to coastlines, reducing warning time
UPSC relevance: RI was a key factor in Cyclone Amphan (2020) and Tauktae (2021) causing forecast challenges

concepts.name: Storm Surge: The Deadliest Component of a Cyclone
key_dimensions: Definition: abnormal rise of sea water above predicted astronomical tide, driven by wind stress and low pressure
Factors determining surge height: cyclone intensity, forward speed, coastal bathymetry, angle of approach, and coastal geometry
UPSC trap: storm surge is NOT the same as a tsunami — different mechanism; surge is wind/pressure-driven, tsunami is seismic
Historical example: 1970 Bhola Cyclone storm surge (~10m) killed ~300,000 — deadliest cyclone on record; policy link to Odisha's cyclone shelters

concepts.name: Extratropical Transition (ETT) of Cyclones
key_dimensions: Process by which a tropical cyclone moves poleward, loses warm-core structure, and acquires cold-core extratropical characteristics
Result: cyclone may EXPAND in size and shift peak winds away from centre — counterintuitive danger
UPSC trap: a cyclone undergoing ETT may be classified as 'weakening' by wind speed metrics but can bring intense rainfall and storm surge to higher latitudes
Relevance to North Indian Ocean: cyclones occasionally affect Pakistan and Iran after ETT

concepts.name: Fujiwhara Effect: Interaction Between Two Adjacent Cyclones
key_dimensions: Definition: when two cyclones of similar size come within ~1300–1500 km, they begin to orbit each other cyclonically
Possible outcomes: mutual orbit and separation, merger into one stronger system, or one absorbing the other
UPSC trap: the Fujiwhara effect does NOT always lead to intensification; can cause weakening or irregular tracks
Recent example: dual cyclone interactions in the Bay of Bengal causing forecast uncertainty — disaster management implication

concepts.name: Medicanes (Mediterranean Hurricanes): A Hybrid Cyclone Type
key_dimensions: Definition: rare, hurricane-like low-pressure systems forming over the Mediterranean Sea with tropical characteristics
Formation: cold upper-level lows interacting with relatively warm Mediterranean SST — hybrid warm/cold core structure
UPSC trap: Medicanes are NOT officially classified as tropical cyclones by WMO; they are 'tropical-like cyclones' — a key distinction
Climate change relevance: increasing frequency projected as Mediterranean SSTs warm; Medicane Daniel (2023) caused Libya floods

concepts.name: Cyclone Track Prediction and the 'Cone of Uncertainty'
key_dimensions: Cone of uncertainty: represents the probable track of the cyclone centre, NOT the full extent of dangerous conditions
UPSC trap: areas OUTSIDE the cone can still experience destructive winds, storm surge, and rainfall — common public misconception exploited in MCQs
Role of numerical weather prediction (NWP) models: GFS (US), ECMWF (European), IMD models — India's investment in supercomputing for forecast improvement
IMD's forecast accuracy improvement: 5-day track forecast error reduced to ~200 km (2020s) from ~500 km (2000s) — policy context

concepts.name: Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and ENSO Influence on Cyclone Activity
key_dimensions: Positive IOD: warmer western Indian Ocean → enhanced Arabian Sea cyclone activity; cooler eastern IO → suppressed Bay of Bengal activity
El Niño: increases vertical wind shear in the Atlantic (suppresses hurricanes) but has a complex, often intensifying effect on Arabian Sea cyclones
La Niña: generally associated with increased Atlantic hurricane activity and active Bay of Bengal cyclone seasons
UPSC trap: ENSO effects on Indian Ocean cyclones are NOT the mirror image of Atlantic effects — direct application of Atlantic ENSO rules to India is a common error

concepts.name: Cyclone Warnings and the NDMA-IMD Early Warning Framework in India
key_dimensions: IMD's four-tier colour-coded alert system for cyclones: Green (watch/awareness) → Yellow → Orange → Red (immediate action)
Cyclone Warning Centres (CWCs) in India: Chennai, Mumbai, Bhubaneswar — each with area of responsibility
UPSC trap: IMD issues warnings but NDMA coordinates response — distinct roles of technical agency vs. disaster management authority under DM Act 2005
72-hour, 48-hour, 24-hour warning milestones and corresponding mandatory evacuation triggers in coastal states

concepts.name: Landfall: Definition, Impacts, and Post-Landfall Weakening
key_dimensions: Landfall defined as the moment the eye/centre crosses the coastline — NOT when the outer bands first reach the coast
Mechanisms of post-landfall weakening: loss of warm ocean energy source, increased surface friction, dry air entrainment
UPSC trap: a cyclone can cause its MAXIMUM damage BEFORE official landfall due to storm surge and outer band rainfall — policy implication for early evacuation
Recurvature phenomenon: North Indian Ocean cyclones often recurve northward/northeastward — why Odisha and West Bengal are disproportionately impacted

concepts.name: Historical Landmark Cyclones and Their Policy Legacy in India
key_dimensions: 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone (wind 260–300 km/h, 10,000+ deaths) → catalyst for India's cyclone shelter programme and early warning investment
2013 Cyclone Phailin vs. 1999 Odisha Cyclone: similar intensity, but <45 deaths in 2013 due to evacuation of 1 million — benchmark for disaster management success
Cyclone Amphan (2020): first Super Cyclonic Storm in Bay of Bengal since 1999; ₹1 lakh crore damage — costliest Indian cyclone
UPSC trap: linking specific cyclones to specific policy/institutional responses (e.g., Phailin → NDMA best practice, Bhola 1970 → Bangladesh's cyclone shelter policy)

concepts.name: Climate Change and Trends in Tropical Cyclone Characteristics
key_dimensions: IPCC consensus: overall global cyclone frequency may decrease or remain stable, but proportion of high-intensity (Cat 4–5) storms will increase
Poleward migration of peak cyclone intensity: storms reaching maximum intensity at higher latitudes due to warmer SSTs extending poleward
Increase in precipitation rates: ~10–15% increase in rainfall within 100 km of cyclone centre projected per IPCC AR6
UPSC trap: 'more cyclones due to climate change' is an OVERSIMPLIFICATION — the nuanced IPCC position is fewer but more intense storms, a distinction frequently tested
